questions.q: In an Azure NSG rule, what does the priority field control?
options: Which subscription billing tier the rule falls under
How many simultaneous connections the rule allows
The evaluation order — lower numbers are evaluated first, and the first match wins
Whether the rule applies to IPv4 or IPv6 traffic
questions.explain: NSG rules run in priority order (100-4096, lower first) and Azure stops at the first match, so priority is what decides which rule actually governs a given packet.

questions.q: Can an AWS Security Group contain an explicit Deny rule?
options: No — a Security Group can only contain Allow rules; everything else is implicitly denied
Yes, but only for outbound traffic
Yes, and Deny rules always take priority over Allow rules
Yes, as long as the rule has a lower priority number than the Allow rules
questions.explain: Security Groups are allow-only. There is no Deny action and no priority field — every SG starts from an implicit deny-all and you add Allow rules on top.

questions.q: Which AWS construct is the real analog to a subnet-level Azure NSG, including support for an explicit Deny?
options: A VPC endpoint policy
An IAM resource policy
A second Security Group attached to the same subnet
A Network ACL (NACL), because it attaches to a subnet, evaluates in rule-number order, and supports explicit Allow and Deny
questions.explain: NACLs, not Security Groups, attach at the subnet level and support explicit Deny — the same model as an NSG's priority-ordered, first-match evaluation.

questions.q: A Security Group rule and a NACL rule are both evaluated in some order. What is the key structural difference between them?
options: NACLs only work with HTTPS traffic; Security Groups work with any protocol
Security Group rules from multiple attached groups are unioned together with no ordering, while NACL rules are evaluated in numbered order with first match winning
NACLs can only be attached to EC2 instances, not subnets
Security Groups require a separate outbound rule for every inbound rule
questions.explain: Because SGs are allow-only, there's nothing to shadow, so rules from every attached SG are simply unioned. NACLs support Deny, so they need an explicit rule-number order to resolve conflicts.

questions.q: What does it mean that NACLs are stateless while Security Groups and NSGs are stateful?
options: Stateless rules expire automatically after 24 hours
A stateless NACL requires a separate, explicit outbound rule to permit return traffic, while a stateful SG or NSG automatically allows the response to an already-permitted connection
Stateful rules can only be written through the CLI, not the console
Stateless rules apply to an entire VPC; stateful rules apply to a single subnet
questions.explain: Statefulness is about return traffic: an SG or NSG Allow rule auto-permits the matching response, but a NACL evaluates inbound and outbound independently, so both directions need their own rule.
